_what: Declarative watch list for the ternary-leg watchdog (.github/workflows/ternary-leg-watchdog.yml).
_why: Monitoring used to live in a background poller inside an agent session. That dies whenever the session or container stops -- twice on 2026-07-25, once silently for 31 minutes on an unbounded curl -- and a long GPU leg then runs unwatched: a spot preemption is not noticed, nothing resumes it, and the wall clock is lost. This file plus the scheduled workflow move the watch OUT of the session entirely. All state lives in the repo and in GCS, so it survives restarts, and no agent needs to be awake.
_how: The workflow runs on a cron. For each enabled entry it asks GCS three questions: is the leg's result JSON already there (done), is the leg ADVANCING (a live VM whose committed iteration is still climbing), or is it dead/stalled? Only a dead leg is re-dispatched, which resumes from the last committed checkpoint. A per-day relaunch counter in GCS caps runaway re-dispatch, and every outcome is an annotation; a stall or a hit cap also FAILS the job so GitHub's own failure notification fires.
_editing: Set enabled=false when a leg is finished or deliberately parked -- do NOT delete the entry, so the history of what was watched stays legible. The watchdog is a no-op with an empty or all-disabled list.
_required_keys_are_enforced: ONE FACT, ONE PLACE: `_required_run_params` is the single authoritative list and `_required_run_params_note` explains it. `_prefix_keying_params` is retained ONLY as a backward-compatible alias, because a copy of watchdog_validate.py held by another session may still read that key; it is a SUBSET (it lacks use_preequil) and must not be treated as the requirement. The workflow validates the list on every pass and refuses to act on an incomplete entry rather than relaunching the wrong thing.

_required_run_params_note: Every parameter the watchdog must REPRODUCE on a relaunch; `_required_run_params` below is the authoritative list. Two classes, both mandatory. (1) PREFIX-KEYING: the spot commit prefix is <seed>_dt<timestep_fs>fs_clig0_wu<warmup_timestep_fs>[_<commit_salt>][_dir<direction>], so omitting one makes the watchdog resume a DIFFERENT trajectory than the one it is watching. (2) NOT prefix-keying but SYSTEM-CHANGING: use_preequil selects whether the alchemy starts from the plain-MD-relaxed physical complex (SETUP_VER=v2pe) or the raw one (v1). CORRECTED 2026-07-25 -- an earlier version of this note claimed pre-equilibration 'only moves coordinates' so 'the particle counts are IDENTICAL' and OpenFE could not catch a v1/v2pe cross-restore. That was never measured and it is FALSE: the prime markers give v1 = 146,020 particles and v2pe = 141,968, because the pre-equilibrated complex is RE-SOLVATED, so assert_multistate_system_equality WOULD reject a cross-restore. Reproducing use_preequil is mandatory for a stronger reason: the setup-cache key carries the version (..._r0__nagl__v1 vs ..._r0__nagl__v2pe), so getting it wrong runs a DIFFERENT SYSTEM, not merely a bad resume. That is what happened: four rev attempts ran the 146,020-particle v1 system against a fwd leg built at 141,968, and all four died at warmup iteration 1. See sections J-J.5 of ternary-lane-guard-audit-2026-07-25.md. ADDED 2026-07-27 -- `restrain`. It is BOTH classes at once, which is why it is mandatory rather than optional: it keys the spot commit prefix (`_rst`) AND the leg result file, and it selects a DIFFERENT HAMILTONIAN (a flat-bottom pocket restraint, ternary_restraint.py). A watchdog that did not carry it would fail twice over on a restrained leg -- the DONE check would `ls` the UNRESTRAINED result, which for the r0 binary arm is ALREADY IN THE BUCKET, and declare a leg finished that had not started; and a relaunch would dispatch restrain=0, quietly starting a different calculation at a different prefix while reporting it as the same leg. Every pre-existing entry was given the explicit default '0' in the same commit, which is what they have always run, so nothing changed behaviourally and no entry was left failing validation.
_relaunch_cap_note: max_relaunches_per_day was 8 and that is a HARD BLOCKER at the observed spot preemption rate. Measured 2026-07-25: two consecutive L4 spot VMs on this leg lasted ~30 min and <=62 min (mean ~45 min). Against 26.4 h of remaining MD that is ~35 VM lifetimes, so a cap of 8 would stop the watchdog relaunching on day one and the leg would sit dead with no GPU running and only a CAPPED annotation to show it. Raised to 40. RAISING IT IS SAFE ONLY BECAUSE the crash detector now separates the two cases: a leg that DIED (no VM, no post-mortem -- preemption) is relaunched and resumes from its last committed checkpoint, while a leg that CRASHED (post-mortem newer than its VM) is reaped and explicitly NOT relaunched. So a deterministic failure cannot spin the counter; only preemptions consume it, and each one resumes rather than restarts. Before the crash detector existed, a low cap was the only thing standing between a repeating crash and a runaway.
_provisioning_note: standard (= ON-DEMAND). **AUTHORIZED BY trimcrae 2026-07-25 ~5:30 PM ET**, which is the authorization gpu-ternary-fep-gcp.yml requires: 'Use standard ONLY when explicitly authorized for a time-sensitive one-off, e.g. confirming a single valB leg'. This is that one-off -- the leg gates the entire valB_mini rescope decision. It is a deliberate, recorded reversal of the standing DEFAULT EVERY GPU RUN TO SPOT rule, and it applies to THIS leg only; new work still defaults to spot. The decision (on-demand beats spot for this leg) is UNCHANGED by the corrections in _rate_appendix below -- a slower true per-iteration cost makes the leg longer, which makes preemption-free wall clock worth MORE, not less. TO REVERT: set this back to 'spot'; the switch takes effect on the next relaunch. NB pricing.md still forbids quoting the L4-on-demand figure as a go-forward COST BASIS for the program; spending stranded credit on one gating leg is a different question from pricing the ladder.
_measured_rate:
TWO NUMBERS, MEASURING DIFFERENT THINGS. Use 59 s/iter for any ETA and 56.5 s/iter when talking about MD cost.
  MD cost, in-log, per-iteration, unquantized (iter_timing_profile.awk SEGMENT lines, GH run 30210933840): production is FLAT at 56.2-57.1 s/iter across 600 consecutive production iterations (56.56, 56.22, 56.62, 56.45, 56.38, 57.14 per 100-iteration block). Warmup on the same VM is 47.2 s/iter. THERE IS NO CREEP -- an earlier reading of 'rises 45.3 -> 56.5 then plateaus' was the warmup->production step, not a drift: this VM restored warmup@200 and ran 200->800, so the profile's 600th timing line IS the phase change, which the driver's own 'restore -> warmup@iter 200' line and the GCS census (warmup complete at 800) both confirm independently.
  WALL cost, end-to-end from the GCS commit-marker series: ~59-60 s/iter (production 80 -> 560 across 479 min of VM life = 59.9). The ~6% over the in-log value is COMMIT+UPLOAD overhead -- a ~25 MB .nc/.chk pair to GCS every 40 production iterations, 12 commits over that window, which is the right order for the gap.
  MARKER RATES ARE QUANTIZATION-LIMITED TO ROUGHLY +/-6% EVEN OVER 8-HOUR WINDOWS, because a marker's position is only known to the nearest 40 iterations and the watchdog polls 20-70 min apart. The same series has yielded 48.5, 56.3, 59.9, 66.0 and 70.5 s/iter over different cuts; NONE of those is a slowdown or a speed-up, and the 70.5 was checked against the in-log profile precisely because it looked like one. Quote the in-log value for MD, add the measured commit overhead for wall clock, and never diagnose a rate change from markers alone.
  Warmup and production run the SAME number of MD steps per iteration (OpenFE fixes n_steps once from the PRODUCTION timestep: 2.5 ps time_per_iteration / 2.0 fs = 1250 steps, and rbfe_spot_driver builds the warmup move as a COPY with only .timestep changed), so the 47.2 -> 56.5 step is NOT step count -- production also writes positions every 20 iterations into a growing .nc. That is a 1.2x difference, not the 1.95x originally chased, and it is why the 33.91 s/iter once on record could not be extrapolated: it was a warmup measurement from a DIFFERENT (spot) VM and matches neither phase here.
_leg_targets: warmup_target=800 (ci=8), prod_target=2000 (ci=40) -- read from the driver's own log line, not derived. prod_target=2000 is production_length 5.0 ns / time_per_iteration 2.5 ps. A full leg is therefore 2800 iterations ~= 44 h of MD at the measured 56.5 s/iter. The on-demand max-run cap in gpu-ternary-fep-gcp.yml is 259200s (72 h), raised 20h -> 40h -> 72h on 2026-07-26 as the arithmetic was actually done: 20h came from a warmup-measured rate, and 40h leaves a FRESH leg one boundary SHORT of finishing. 604800s (7 d) is also accepted at create but deliberately unused -- no leg exceeds ~44 h. THE CAP CAN ONLY BE SET AT CREATE: GCP refuses to change max-run-duration on a running instance (gcp-gpu-facts.md 3b), so a cap set too low is a boundary already bought. Each boundary costs 2-4 h of dead wall clock because recovery depends on the watchdog cron, which GitHub delivers at ~2-4 h intervals for this repo whatever the expression says -- dispatching the watchdog by hand the moment the VM disappears turns that into minutes.
_rate_appendix: SUPERSEDED NUMBERS, kept because they stay quotable and CI needs to find copies (CLAUDE.md rule 1.2). (a) '33.91 s/iter' and the derived '106.2 iter/h': a WARMUP measurement from the earlier spot attempts, applied to the whole leg. The true cost is 60.5 s/iter end-to-end -- 1.78x -- so every duration derived from it was ~44% too short. (b) 'the remaining 2704 iterations are ~48 h of calendar on spot vs ~25.5 h un-preempted, so ~23 h saved': built on (a); the un-preempted figure for 2704 iterations at 60.5 s/iter is ~45 h, not 25.5 h. (c) '~2 VM lifetimes instead of ~35' for the 20 h cap: the 20 h cap could never span a ~40 h leg, so it was always >=2 VMs and the comment in gpu-ternary-fep-gcp.yml claiming 20 h 'spans the WHOLE run uninterrupted' was wrong; corrected there and the cap raised to 40 h. (d) 'COST: ~$10 of GCP trial credit': that was one 20 h VM at the old rate estimate. Actual exposure for the whole leg is ~40-46 h of on-demand L4 ~= $30-40 of TRIAL CREDIT, $0 cash, on credit that expires 2026-10-10 and is otherwise stranded. (e) a reading of 'production/280' taken at 8:01 AM 2026-07-26 was reported as ~299 in a status message; the marker series is 80/120/120/200/240/240/280/320 and was monotonic throughout -- there was no regression, the 299 was simply wrong. (f) an ETA of 'Mon 9:30 AM - 12:40 PM ET' derived from (a) is withdrawn; see _eta. (g) '60.5 s/iter', which this file carried for a few hours on 2026-07-26: correct arithmetic over the window available at the time (production 80 -> 320 across 242 min) but a SHORT window, and marker quantization dominates those -- the same series yields 66.0 s/iter and 48.5 s/iter over two other sub-windows. Superseded by 56.5 s/iter, which is the in-log per-iteration plateau and is corroborated to 0.3% by the long-window marker rate (80 -> 440 across 338 min = 56.3 s/iter). Not a measurement error, a window-length error; the lesson is to quote the unquantized in-log value and use markers only to corroborate it. (h) an ETA of 'Mon 3:20 PM - 5:20 PM ET' derived from (g) is withdrawn; see _eta. (i) '~68 iter/h (52.8 s/iter)', which nr4a3-program-map.md's schedule row carried: a WARMUP-window figure from two short baselines (63 min and 190 min), and a fourth value for this one fact -- 33.91, 52.8, 60.5 and 56.5 were all live in the repo at once, which is precisely the failure CLAUDE.md rule 1 exists to stop. Superseded by 56.5 s/iter. That row now POINTS here instead of restating, along with its stale 'warmup/640' position and its '~Mon 8:40 AM' ETA. (j) 'Mon 1:10 PM - 3:10 PM ET', quoted at 11:02 AM: derived from 56.5 s/iter used as a WALL rate, when it is the MD-only rate. Adding the measured ~6% commit+upload overhead gives ~59 s/iter and moves completion ~1.5 h later. (k) a 70.5 s/iter reading over the last 141 min was NOT a slowdown -- it was marker quantization, and the in-log SEGMENT profile (flat 56.2-57.1 s/iter over 600 production iterations) is what established that. Recorded because the check is the point: a 25% apparent slowdown on a billed leg had to be either confirmed or killed with data, not waved off as noise. (l) the 40 h cap set at ~9 AM 2026-07-26, described then as removing a VM boundary: it removes one for the RUNNING leg (which needs only ~22 h more) but NOT for a fresh leg, which needs ~44 h. Raised to 72 h once the leg length was computed rather than assumed. (m) 'Mon 2:45 PM - 4:45 PM ET', quoted before the boundary: it budgeted 2-4 h of cron detection latency for the VM boundary. The cron actually fired 5 min after the cap expired, so the boundary cost ~8 min and the estimate was ~2 h pessimistic. The measured ~2-4 h cadence is an AVERAGE, not a bound -- it can fire promptly, and budgeting the average as a worst case overstates the loss. The hand-dispatch precaution was still correct: it was armed for the case that did not happen, and cost nothing when it did not. (n) 'Mon 12:00 PM - 3:00 PM', widened at 5:43 PM on a cumulative marker rate of 66 s/iter that suggested the new VM might be ~10% slower: it was not. The in-log profile gives 56.7 s/iter, identical to the old VM. The 66 s/iter was marker quantisation plus the resume cycle -- and at the check before that I called a 59.5 s/iter marker reading a '1% match' to the recorded rate, which overstated precision that window (120 iterations, +/-33%) could not support. BOTH readings were noise around the same true value. The standing rule already said not to diagnose a rate from markers; I did it twice in consecutive checks, in both directions.
_eta: As of 5:47 PM ET Sun 2026-07-26 on the post-boundary VM gcp-ternary-30215419909 (us-central1-a, 72 h cap, dies_in ~4140 min -- NO FURTHER BOUNDARY). _gcp_cost_frame:
★ ON GCP, MONEY IS NOT THE CONSTRAINT — WALL CLOCK IS (trimcrae, 2026-07-26: 'as long as you're using GCP it's all free credits that we're trying to burn through so don't hesitate on account of price'). The trial credit expires 2026-10-10 and is otherwise a stranded asset, so unspent credit is a LOSS, not a saving. Three things follow, and they reverse the usual reflex:
  1. ON-DEMAND IS THE DEFAULT ON GCP, not an authorised exception. It cannot be preempted and gets a longer      max-run cap, and both of those buy WALL CLOCK, which is the scarce thing. The standing 'DEFAULT EVERY GPU      RUN TO SPOT' rule is about REAL money and still governs Vast and AWS unchanged.
  2. THE REAL CEILING IS THE QUOTA. GPUS_ALL_REGIONS = 1 (gcp-gpu-facts.md #1) caps the project at ONE      concurrent GPU regardless of the per-type quotas (the regional PREEMPTIBLE_NVIDIA_L4_GPUS limit is 3 and      sits unused because of it). ⚠ CORRECTED 2026-07-27 — THE DOLLAR CEILING BINDS FIRST, AND THE QUOTA IS NOT A LEVER. This said the quota was the bottleneck and that credit could not all be burned; both halves were wrong. 1 GPU x 24 h x ~76 days is ~1,824 GPU-h of WALL CLOCK, but the credit only covers ~411 L4-h (~$292 at ~$0.71/L4-h) — so ~1,824 GPU-h was never purchasable and the asset was overstated ~4.4x. MONEY RUNS OUT BEFORE THE CALENDAR DOES, which reverses this section's own headline for any spend large enough to matter. And 'raise GPUS_ALL_REGIONS' is NOT an available action: trimcrae has requested it repeatedly and been refused (small account), and at quota 4 the same $292 is simply spent 4x faster, so it would not have bought more science even if granted. ONE HOME for this arithmetic — STRATEGY.md Appendix A row 20 and its runway table (~411 L4-h ~= 17 days continuous ~= 9.4 full legs at 43.9 L4-h/leg); do not restate it here. Treat the 1-GPU cap as a FIXED property of the lane: GCP is the always-on SERIAL worker whose idle time is expiring credit, Vast is burst capacity bought when wall clock is the scarce thing.
  3. COST-BASED REASONING IN THIS LANE'S COMMENTS IS NOW WRONG BY DEFAULT. A larger max-run cap, a longer      leg, an extra diagnostic run: none of these has a price worth weighing on GCP. Weigh them against wall      clock and the single-GPU serialisation instead. NB pricing.md's separate rule still stands and is about a      different question: never quote the L4-on-demand figure as a go-forward COST BASIS for the program,      because that prices a future funded programme rather than this expiring credit.
_requires_watchdog_features_note: A CAPABILITY HANDSHAKE, not documentation. watchdog_run.sh declares WATCHDOG_FEATURES and REFUSES to act (exit 1 + ::error) if this list asks for anything it does not implement. It exists because an older watchdog reading a newer entry does not error -- it silently drops the field it does not know and then measures the WRONG ARTIFACT: without restraint_keyed_result_v1 a restrain=1 entry resolves the UNRESTRAINED result key, which for the r0 binary arm is ALREADY IN THE BUCKET, so it reports a green DONE for a leg that never ran and leaves that leg's VM holding GPUS_ALL_REGIONS=1 while billing. SCOPE, honestly: ternary-leg-watchdog.yml's actions/checkout@v4 takes NO ref, so the script and this file normally travel together and cannot diverge. The paths this guards are a SELECTIVE MERGE forwarding this JSON without the script, and the divergent private copies noted in _required_keys_are_enforced. It CANNOT protect against a watchdog older than the handshake itself, which never reads this key. Pinned by tests/test_watchdog_restraint_guards.sh.
